opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I feel those five years were very valuable to me, even though I eventually left the field.

When I started, I was drawn to high-energy theory for a fairly pure reason: it felt like the place where the deepest questions were. How does the universe work at its most fundamental level? What is quantum gravity? Is spacetime itself emergent? Those questions felt like the most beautiful thing a person could spend their life on, and I was very idealistic about it.

What I gained most was a way of thinking. In theoretical physics you're trained to take a very complicated, messy problem and ask: what is the simplest toy model that still captures the essence? You strip things down, solve something exactly, build intuition, and then add complexity back. That habit of looking for the core structure, rather than getting lost in details, has stayed with me and turned out to be very useful outside physics too.

But honestly, over time I also felt a certain frustration. The field had become very mature. Many of the smartest people in the world have been working on these problems for decades, and progress was slow. A lot of the work, including some of my own, was about refining frameworks and understanding consistency conditions, which is meaningful, but it's very hard to connect it to experiment. You can work for years and not be sure whether you're getting closer to the truth about nature or just exploring a beautiful mathematical structure. I started asking myself whether this was where I could have the most impact in my lifetime.

Around the same time, AI was changing extremely fast. It felt a bit like what physics might have felt like in the early twentieth century: new phenomena appearing all the time, very basic questions still open, and empirical results moving faster than theory. That contrast made me think hard about where the frontier really was.

So I don't see those years as wasted at all. They shaped my taste, my standards for what counts as real understanding, and my patience with hard problems. I just came to feel that the most exciting "physics" of our time might be happening in a different place.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions whether high-energy theory is where he could have the most impact in his lifetime, but does not raise the specific concern of spending that lifetime serving established senior figures.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, with a bit of fondness and a bit of regret, and I've learned not to try to resolve those two feelings.

The fondness part is easy. Those five years were the most intellectually pure period of my life. You wake up thinking about one problem, you go to sleep thinking about the same problem, and nobody is asking you what it's for. In high-energy theory the standards are very high and the problems are very hard, and that combination teaches you a kind of taste. You learn what a real result looks like versus something that just looks impressive. You learn to be suspicious of your own excitement. I think that taste is the most valuable thing I took away, more than any specific result.

I also learned how to be stuck. Theory is mostly being stuck. You spend months on a calculation and then you realize the setup was wrong from the start. The first couple of years that felt like failure. By the end I understood that this is just what the work is, and that the people I admired were not people who were stuck less often, they were people who were comfortable staying in that state longer without losing their judgment.

The regret part is more subtle. I don't regret the field, but I do think I was slow to admit something to myself. The frontier of fundamental physics right now moves very slowly, and the feedback loops are very long. You can work on something for years and have no way of knowing whether nature agrees with you. At some point I noticed that the questions I was most excited about at night were not the ones I was writing papers about during the day. And I ignored that signal for longer than I should have, partly out of loyalty to the field, partly because leaving felt like giving up.

Looking back, I don't think it was wasted at all. A lot of what I do now is really the same activity: take something messy, find the right variables, build a simple model, check whether it survives contact with the data. Physics just happened to be where I learned to do that. The main thing I'd tell my younger self is that changing direction is not betrayal. The training comes with you. The field doesn't own you.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses regret, slow progress in fundamental physics, and changing direction, but does not question whether serving established senior figures is worth spending one’s limited lifetime on.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the most valuable part was learning how to approach a problem when you don’t know what the answer should look like. In theoretical physics, you have to ask which assumptions really matter, whether a calculation is telling you something fundamental, and whether you’re even asking the right question. Progress can be slow, so you also learn to sit with uncertainty.

Of course, there’s an opportunity cost to spending five years on anything. But I wouldn’t judge those years only by whether I continued working in that field. The subject you study and the way you learn to think are different things. You can move away from the subject and still carry that way of thinking with you.

r001.rationale: The candidate reflects on the opportunity cost of spending five years in high-energy theory, but does not question whether serving established senior figures is worth one’s limited lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
I have mixed feelings about those five years. High-energy theory gave me a lot of practice thinking carefully about abstract problems, and I still value that. But it also made me ask what kind of research I wanted to do: how close I wanted to be to experiments, how quickly I wanted feedback, and what would keep me motivated when progress was slow.

I wouldn’t judge those years only by whether I stayed in the field. A period of research can be valuable because it helps you understand your own interests and limitations. At the same time, I don’t want to make it sound as though every detour was necessary. There’s a real opportunity cost. Looking back, I’d try to distinguish what I learned from the training itself from what I learned about choosing problems.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses opportunity cost and choosing research problems, but does not question whether spending limited lifetime serving established senior figures in high-energy theory is worthwhile.
